newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Clinton seeks to change controversial FDR memorial.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Clinton seeks to change controversial FDR memorial.

text.p: Bowing to appeals from disabled Americans, President Bill Clinton has agreed to ask Congress to modify a memorial to Franklin Roosevelt to include a statue of the 32nd president in a wheelchair.

Roosevelt spent his presidency in a wheelchair but, to the anguish of some handicapped Americans, the new memorial's current design obscures that fact. A White House statement on Wednesday said Clinton would submit legislation to modify the memorial "so that generations of Americans will know that this great president was great with his disability."

Hundreds of wheelchair-bound protestors had threatened to demonstrate when the memorial is unveiled on May 2 unless Clinton, himself temporarily on crutches, intervened to get a portrayal of Roosevelt in a wheelchair added to the statuary.

Roosevelt, who led the United States out of the Depression of the 1930s and through most of the Second World War, was paralysed from the waist down by polio at age 39, years before he entered the White House. But he insisted his handicap be disguised in most public appearances.
NO SCULPTURE OF FDR IN WHEELCHAIR

The $48 million memorial is a series of four outdoor rooms containing bronze sculptures and granite walls with quotations from Roosevelt's four terms in office. There is a sculpture of him on a chair with small wheels attached to the legs, but it is not a wheelchair. There is also an empty replica of one of his wheelchairs and a photograph of him in a wheelchair.

Clinton's action would instruct Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt to come up with plans for design and construction of an additional statue, bas relief, or similar sculpture of Roosevelt in his wheelchair. Clinton joined 16 of Roosevelt's grandchildren, as well as former presidents George Bush, Jimmy Carter and Gerald Ford, in calling for a permanent depiction of FDR's disability at the memorial.

Before the White House statement was released, Dick Thornburgh, a former U.S. attorney general who is a lawyer for Deland's group, had expressed hope that Clinton's sympathy might be spurred by the fact he is now on crutches. "It is kind of a felicitous coincidence," he said.

Clinton, who had surgery on March 14 to repair a torn right knee tendon, attended a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in a wheelchair the following week but quickly graduated to the crutches he will use for several months.
DISABLED ASKED FOR SCULPTURE TWO YEARS AGO

Groups representing the disabled asked the memorial commission two years ago to depict Roosevelt in a wheelchair in one of the sculptures, but the panel voted to keep the existing design. Commission representatives then said it would take an act of Congress to change the design, but Thornburgh said legal research did not support that. He said additions were made to the Vietnam War memorial without an act of Congress and the decision was ultimately Clinton's.

A grandson of Roosevelt, Christopher duPont Roosevelt, had also expressed hope that Clinton would help. The New York lawyer said he had been impressed with Clinton's statement on March 27, after his knee surgery, about life as a disabled person: "The dignity and the strength of character that it takes to kind of organise your life ... is enormous."

Asked what he thought his grandfather would have wanted as a memorial, Roosevelt said the grand new tribute already had disregarded FDR's wish for a humble monument, but he thought FDR would sympathise with the disabled groups.
"I think he would understand that a memorial that fails to adequately describe the process in his life that most likely contributed the most to his character is not right."
